title: Hillel's seven rules
hook: Hillel's rules for reading Torah, later expanded to thirteen

segments.voice: Yesterday, gezerah shavah: a bridge between verses, received from teachers, never made up on a whim. Your line: same word, same law. Today, the man who put that bridge on a list.

The day before Passover falls on Shabbat, and the leaders of the day, the sons of Bathyra, are stuck. They can't remember whether the Passover offering pushes aside the rules of Shabbat. Someone mentions a newcomer up from Babylonia, a student of the great teachers of the age. They send for him. His name is Hillel. He walks in and starts reasoning: a bridge from a shared word, a light-and-heavy argument, one move after another. They aren't moved. Then he says one more sentence, and everything changes.
screen: `PASSOVER MEETS SHABBAT.` → `SEND FOR THE NEWCOMER.` → `HILLEL REASONS. NO ONE MOVES.`

segments.voice: Hillel's seven rules. You met Hillel back in year one; today, his toolbox. The Tosefta, an early collection beside the Mishnah, says Hillel expounded seven rules of reading before the sons of Bathyra. Two you already know: light and heavy, and the same word. Others build a general principle from one verse, or from two; read a general statement together with its particulars; compare a case to a similar one elsewhere; and learn a thing from its context. Take that last one, because it's easy to feel. The Ten Commandments say, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "Thou shalt not steal." Ordinary theft is forbidden elsewhere in the Torah. So what is this line doing here? Look at its neighbors: murder and adultery, crimes the Torah treats as capital. The Talmud reads it from its context as stealing a person, kidnapping. Same line, read by the company it keeps. Now the rest of the story. In the Jerusalem Talmud's telling, Hillel's arguments don't move the sons of Bathyra. Then he says: this is what I heard from my teachers, Shemaya and Avtalyon. And they accept him, and make him their leader. Yesterday's limit, lived out: the rules matter, and so does the chain of teachers they come down through. Later comes a longer list: a teaching at the start of the Sifra gives Rabbi Ishmael's thirteen rules, with Hillel's tools among them. Some traditional prayer books print that list in the morning service, so the tools of reading sit right beside the prayers.
screen: `SEVEN RULES BEFORE THE ELDERS.` · `LEARN A THING FROM ITS CONTEXT.` · `WHAT I HEARD FROM MY TEACHERS.` · `LATER, RABBI ISHMAEL'S THIRTEEN.` · then, large: `RULES FOR READING.`

segments.voice: Bring back one sentence someone said to you recently that stung or puzzled you, and hold the words alone for a moment. Then widen the frame: what came right before it, and what kind of day were they having? Notice whether the sentence changes when it has its neighbors back.
Hillel's seven rules. Seven ways of reading Torah that the Tosefta credits to Hillel, from light and heavy to learning from context, later built on by Rabbi Ishmael's thirteen. Today's word.
Your line: rules for reading. The tools and the teachers came down together. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some traditional prayer books print Rabbi Ishmael's thirteen rules for reading Torah in the morning service, and students of rabbinic literature learn to recognize each rule as it appears in the Talmud and midrash.

chat.says: How did Hillel finally win over the sons of Bathyra?
options: Not by argument alone: they accepted him when he said he'd heard it from his teachers.
He cast lots, and the elders agreed to accept whatever answer the lots gave.
He showed them a written book of laws that settled the question on the spot.

'Ordinary theft is forbidden elsewhere in the Torah' refers to Leviticus 19:11; the kidnapping reading is cited to Sanhedrin 86a. Please confirm.

Editor: in Bavli Pesachim 66a the Bnei Betera appoint Hillel nasi right after his arguments; the version where the arguments fail until he cites Shemaya and Avtalyon is the Jerusalem Talmud, Pesachim 6:1. The voice, myth and fork now say 'the Jerusalem Talmud's telling', and that source was added. 'Elders of Bathyra' changed to 'sons of Bathyra' (bnei Betera) throughout; 'in Jerusalem' cut from the hook; Rabbi Ishmael's list no longer said to be 'building on' Hillel's, and the prayer-book claim softened to 'some traditional prayer books'.
